newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Playwright Dorfman confronts past in new play.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Playwright Dorfman confronts past in new play.

text.p: When Ariel Dorfman was exiled from Chile in 1973 by the coup that brought General Augusto Pinochet to power, he was was so disturbed he could not write drama or prose for 2-1/2 years.
Exile was a form of death for the playwright who finally confronted his traumatic experiences in "Death and the Maiden".
The story of three people's brutal experiences in a coup in an unnamed Latin American country earned him worldwide fame and was made into a film starring Sigourney Weaver and Ben Kingsley.
"If you do not confront the past you will carry it with you forever and it will bring you down," Dorfman told Reuters in an interview. "Writing brought me back to myself."
In his new play, Dorfman again tries to exorcise his past.

"Widows" is the story of the wives and daughters of the "disappeared" who, under the grip of totalitarianism, wait for their beloved husbands and fathers to return. Like "Death and the Maiden" it is based in an unnamed Latin American country.
Dorfman, 55, believes the play speaks for repression in many countries.

"I think this play, 'Widows', could stand in for so many tormented places around the world, not only people," he said. "I am trying to find the common humanity that we share. I have tried to situate the play in a mythical, legendary landscape."
He said one of the problems he confronted in his years of silence was finding a way to make his work accessible to people who had not shared his experience.
He cited the conflicts in Bosnia, East Timor, Rwanda and countries undergoing the transition to democracy as countries where the 'Widows' scenario could be directly transposed.
PINOCHET'S INFLUENCE
But Dorfman does not doubt the influence of Pinochet's government on his work.

"The repression by General Pinochet and the destruction of everything I believed in and the pain inflicted in my country and so many of my friends and family, has been the central traumatic experience of my life," he said.
"I would say my play (Widows) is like a burial ground, I'm burying my dead because the generals won't let me."

Dorfman called on the services of Ian Brown, who helped produce his play "Readers", to direct "Widows". The pair have revamped the play for its production by the Traverse Theatre company, adding a narrator who acts as Dorfman's mouthpiece on stage.
In the first act the narrator proclaims :"Exile is like death," an analogy Dorfman said described his own experience in Chile.
"Exile in my case acted as a form of death. I lived through a transition of death. But it was also an inspiration, it made me think," he said.

'Widows' is a play which displays very real violence because, Dorfman said, "that's what happens." His plays are deliberately provocative and jerk his audiences from the amnesia which he says accompanies the transition to democracy.
They do not act as a personal catharsis as he is still clearly disturbed by his past.

"I did not chose to write about these things, violence chose me. I would have been very happy not to have written these plays because if I had not, the situations which inspired them would have been non-existent."
Dorfman admitted to dealing with situations that are extreme but distinguished them from what he called everyday "pop-violence" on television.
"I have lived very near this violence," he said. "I can either succumb to it or make drama out of it."
But he is not entirely free from self-censure. "Violence does make for good drama."
DORFMAN HOPES "WIDOWS" WILL BE FILMED
Dorfman divides his time between the United States, where he holds a professorship at Duke University, North Carolina, and Chile which he said he hopes to visit for three months this year.
He would love to repeat the success of "Death and the Maiden" and make "Widows" into a film -- he said a leading British actor has shown an interest in making it.

But he doubted whether a studio would want to take in on. "I think, frankly, people are not very interested in illiterate old peasant women. They're not flashy, they're not sexy and they're not middle class."

People want to be uplifted by film, Dorfman said, which would make it difficult to attract financing. Though "Death and the Maiden" attracted studio interest, he said it took several years just to raise the money to put "Widows" on stage.

"Death and the Maiden" tells the story of a woman who relives the nightmare of her rape and torture in a military coup, when a her husband innocently offers a man shelter from a storm in their home. She claims the man raped and abused her when she was held by the regime and a menacing mock-trial ensues.
"I don't write about the state and power, I write about human beings," Dorfman said.
As an extension of this, Dorfman leaves the ending of "Widows" open as a way of forcing the audience to decide what happens.
"I love to do that, I call it the democracy of the spectator," he said, adding with a laugh."Others would call it the cowardice of the playwright."
